title: Oraciones de relativo para precisar información

sections.content: Relative clauses let one sentence carry a definition, an attribution, or an ownership relationship without starting a new sentence — que for things and people, a quienes for people as an object, cuyo/cuya/cuyos/cuyas for 'whose,' agreeing with the thing possessed, not the possessor. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: Durante siglos se habló de 'descubrimiento', una palabra que asumía que América no existía realmente hasta que Europa la encontró.
items.english: For centuries people spoke of 'discovery,' a word that assumed America didn't really exist until Europe found it.

items.spanish: Los primeros cálculos fueron publicados por historiadores a quienes hoy se llama 'contadores bajos'.
items.english: The first estimates were published by historians who today are called 'low counters'.

items.spanish: Investigaciones posteriores, cuyos autores revisaron fuentes coloniales con más detalle, elevaron esa cifra a cien millones.
items.english: Later research, whose authors reviewed colonial sources in more detail, raised that figure to a hundred million.

items.spanish: Un ejemplo célebre es la Virgen de Guadalupe, cuya aparición se sitúa en 1531 en el cerro del Tepeyac.
items.english: A famous example is the Virgin of Guadalupe, whose appearance is placed in 1531 on Tepeyac hill.

sections.content: Cuyo agrees with the noun that comes right after it (the thing owned), never with the person it refers back to: cuyos autores (whose authors — because autores is masculine plural), cuya aparición (whose appearance — because aparición is feminine singular). This trips up a lot of learners because English 'whose' never changes form.
